source.title: Benign Overfitting and Grokking in ReLU Networks for XOR Cluster Data
source.authors: Zhiwei Xu; Yutong Wang; Spencer Frei; Gal Vardi; Wei Hu

record.tranche_reason: The paper theoretically analyzes training on label-flipped data and measures training and test error, using XOR cluster data rather than the original image settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical guarantees for one fixed, bounded noise rate and experiments at a fixed 5% noise rate. It does not sweep noise fractions, compare training time with true labels, or test unstructured inputs, explicit regularizers, or the learning order of real and random labels. Cited results from other studies are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study bears directly on V6: under its XOR assumptions, the network fits every clean and flipped training label after one GD step, before learning generalizable cluster features. This reverses the proposed learning order. Completely random labeling in V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: under the stated XOR assumptions, GD first fits all clean and flipped training labels with near-chance clean-test performance, then learns generalizable features while retaining perfect training accuracy. The theoretical guarantee covers a bounded training-time interval.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient descent on synthetic XOR cluster data with a constant fraction of flipped labels; the original claim concerns standard deep networks trained on images with completely random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that a smaller step size delays both overfitting and generalization (R4).

fits_no_version.finding: The network perfectly interpolates partially corrupted XOR training data and later achieves near-zero clean-test error without explicit regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient descent can exhibit benign overfitting and grokking on structured, partially corrupted data without explicit regularization.

record.problems: The theoretical results require high-dimensional XOR cluster data and assumptions A1–A6, including a bounded noise rate and a limited training-time interval; the experiments use 100 runs at a fixed 5% noise rate, with plotted accuracies rather than reported numerical summaries. No controls are reported for these results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results were left out. Related-work findings cited from other papers were excluded.

untested.parts: Completely random training labels, chance test performance under that labeling, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters relative to true-label training.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels and convergence as corruption increases. Comparing two step sizes does not test these predictions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or unstructured Gaussian-noise inputs. Gaussian clusters retain class structure.

The joint corruption-response trajectory: perfect training fit and steadily increasing test error from no corruption to fully random labels. The theorem covers only bounded noise rates; experiments fix the flipping rate at 5%.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization. Unregularized grokking alone does not test these comparisons.
Learning order for completely random labels and for standard image datasets; the demonstrated reversal concerns partially corrupted synthetic XOR data.

missing.what: Direct feature-learning evidence supporting the reversed order: the first-step network approximates a nongeneralizing linear classifier, while later neuron weights align with the class-relevant cluster means. Record this separately from train/test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 limits_scope verdict mistakes an untested condition—completely random labeling—for a demonstrated limitation. Partial label corruption is deliberately introduced as a memorization probe; the network is trained with ordinary logistic loss rather than a special memorization objective.

versions.untested_parts: The guarantees concern a constant fraction of flipped labels under the paper’s assumptions, not labels made completely random; the empirical tests use 5% noise.
The paper uses a fixed noise rate and does not sweep corruption from none to all or report a steady rise in test error.
The paper reports grokking without explicit regularization, but does not test weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or whether removing them harms generalization.
The paper does not test whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network of width m
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on logistic loss after a constant fraction of training labels are flipped; evaluate at t = 1.
rows.measure: Training accuracy and test error on clean-label distribution
rows.value: All training datapoints are correctly classified; test error is between 1/2(1 − n^−Ω(1)) and 1/2(1 + n^−Ω(1)).
rows.uncertainty: With probability at least 1 − n^−Ω(1) − O(1/√m) over data generation and initialization.
rows.note: The training set includes clean and flipped labels. This is a theoretical guarantee under the stated assumptions, not a result on image data or fully randomized labels.
rows.check: The theorem concerns bounded label-flipping noise, not completely random labeling, so remove V1. At t = 1, all noisy labels are already fitted while clean-distribution test error remains near 1/2; together with R2 and the feature analysis, this establishes the reversed learning order.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network of width m
rows.operation_detail: Continue gradient descent on logistic loss after the same label-flipping intervention.
rows.measure: Training accuracy and test error on clean-label distribution
rows.value: All training datapoints remain correctly classified; test error is at most exp(−Ω(n^2.01)).
rows.uncertainty: With probability at least 1 − n^−Ω(1) − O(1/√m).
rows.note: Guarantee holds only over the stated training-time interval and under the paper’s assumptions.
rows.check: Remove V1. Read jointly with R1: generalizable features emerge after the network has already fitted all noisy labels. The reported training fit and clean-test error bound are correctly transcribed.
